blueprint.title: Variable-Length Integer Frame Recovery
blueprint.scenario: A small in-house telemetry daemon encodes sensor readings into a compact binary frame format using variable-length integers (varints) and length-prefixed fields. The codebase lives in /app/codec/ (~1400 lines across encoder, decoder, framer, and a ring-buffer accumulator). The format was hand-rolled to save flash space on a constrained MCU and the spec is in /app/docs/frame_spec.md. A batch of production frame dumps arrived that the decoder silently corrupts or drops on certain inputs, but unit tests on the bundled samples all pass.
blueprint.instruction_draft: Hey — the frame decoder at /app/codec/ is silently mangling some of our production captures. The samples in /app/testdata/ all pass, but when we feed it real captures from /app/captures/ the recovered sensor values are wrong or records get dropped entirely. The format spec is in /app/docs/frame_spec.md. Fix the decoder so it correctly recovers every valid frame from any conforming byte stream, rejects every malformed one without crashing, and writes recovered records to stdout as newline-delimited JSON with fields exactly matching the spec. The fix should be a proper refactor — not just patching the sample cases.
requirements: Decoder correctly decodes all valid frames from any conforming byte stream per /app/docs/frame_spec.md
Malformed frames (bad magic, truncated varint, length-prefix overflow, wrong checksum) are rejected with a non-zero per-frame error indicator without crashing the decoder
Recovered records are written to stdout as newline-delimited JSON with field names matching the spec exactly
Decoder handles frames that span ring-buffer wrap boundaries correctly
Signed varint fields (zigzag-encoded) are decoded with the correct sign
Multi-byte varint continuation bytes are handled correctly at the 4-byte and 7-byte boundary (values near 2^28 and 2^49)
Frame checksum (Adler-32 per spec) is verified across the entire payload including the length-prefix bytes
Decoder does not treat a 0x00 payload byte as a stream terminator
environment: /app/codec/ contains ~1400 lines of Python across: encoder.py (reference, correct), decoder.py (buggy), framer.py (ring-buffer accumulator with wrap logic), accumulator.py, and cli.py

/app/docs/frame_spec.md contains the full binary format specification: magic bytes (0xAB 0xCD), 1-byte version, unsigned varint payload-length, payload (field-tag + varint pairs, signed fields zigzag-encoded), 4-byte Adler-32 checksum covering everything after magic through end of payload
/app/testdata/ contains 6 hand-crafted sample frames that all decode correctly (they avoid all the edge cases)
/app/captures/ contains 4 real binary capture files from production MCUs that trigger the bugs

Planted bugs in decoder.py: (1) zigzag decode uses arithmetic right shift on unsigned integer instead of proper zigzag formula, so negative sensor values have wrong sign; (2) multi-byte varint loop stops at 4 continuation bytes max instead of 7, silently truncating values >= 2^28; (3) Adler-32 checksum computation starts accumulation after the length-prefix bytes, omitting them from the check — so frames with corrupt length fields pass; (4) framer.py ring-buffer wrap: when a frame header spans the wrap boundary the second magic byte is re-read from index 0 instead of 1, causing the frame to be dropped
A correct reference encoder is included so the solver can generate test vectors by encoding known values and verifying round-trips
The cli.py entry point reads a binary file path as argv[1], feeds it through the framer and decoder, and prints JSON records; this is what the verifier calls
pip install nothing needed; stdlib only
blueprint.internal_hint: Root causes: (1) zigzag bug — in decoder.py the signed field decode does `(n >> 1) ^ -(n & 1)` but on an already-int Python value without masking, so for large unsigned n the XOR produces wrong results; correct formula is `(n >> 1) ^ -(n & 1)` applied after treating n as unsigned 64-bit. (2) varint loop — the loop `for _ in range(4)` only reads 4 continuation bytes (5 bytes total = 35 bits) but the spec allows 7 continuation bytes (8 bytes = 56-bit payload length); values >= 2^28 silently lose high bits. (3) Adler-32 — the checksum function is called on `payload` but the spec says it covers `version_byte + length_prefix_bytes + payload`; frames with a length field of 255 that expand to multi-byte varints will pass an incorrect checksum. (4) framer wrap — in framer.py `_find_magic` when the ring buffer wraps it compares buf[wrap_pos] and buf[(wrap_pos+1) % size] but the index arithmetic has an off-by-one so the second byte comes from position 0 of the new data instead of 1. A skilled engineer: runs the cli on the captures, sees some records produce wrong sensor values (sign-flipped deltas), some frames silently vanish near buffer wrap, some oversized frames truncate silently, and some structurally corrupt frames pass. They write a round-trip harness using encoder.py to generate edge-case frames, observe the failures, and trace each one to its decoder.py or framer.py location.
blueprint.trap: A naive solver reads decoder.py, spots the zigzag formula (it looks plausible), runs /app/testdata/ samples (all pass), and submits. The hidden corpus includes: frames with negative sensor deltas (zigzag failure), frames with payload length 268435456 (2^28, varint truncation), frames where the header spans a 4096-byte ring-buffer wrap boundary (framer drop), and frames with a corrupt length field that should fail the checksum but pass the naive Adler-32 (checksum scope bug). All four failure modes must be fixed independently; fixing one or two still fails 60%+ of the corpus.
tests: Round-trip test: encode 50 records with random field values including negative deltas and magnitudes up to 2^40, decode the resulting byte stream, verify every field matches exactly
Zigzag corpus: 20 frames with sensor_delta values -1, -127, -128, -32768, -2147483648; verify decoded JSON has correct negative integers
Large varint corpus: frames with payload_length of 127, 128, 16383, 16384, 2097151, 2097152, 268435455, 268435456; verify all decode without truncation
Checksum corpus: valid frames and frames with one bit flipped in the length-prefix bytes; verify valid frames accepted, corrupt frames rejected with error indicator
Ring-buffer wrap corpus: 10 frames sized so the 2-byte magic header falls exactly on the ring-buffer boundary at offsets 4090-4095 into a 4096-byte buffer; verify frames are recovered not dropped
Null-byte payload corpus: frames whose payload contains 0x00 bytes mid-stream; verify decoder does not terminate early
Malformed corpus: 15 inputs with truncated varints, bad magic, payload shorter than length-prefix claims, version byte != 1; verify all produce per-frame error without crash
Mixed stream: a single byte stream concatenating 200 valid and 30 malformed frames interleaved; verify exactly 200 JSON records emitted and 30 errors, order preserved

verifier_knob.name: corpus_size
verifier_knob.effect: Reducing to 50 frames covering only 4 categories (omitting large-varint and checksum-scope) makes it possible to pass by fixing only the zigzag and wrap bugs; increasing to 500 with additional boundary values (e.g. 2^49-1 varints, back-to-back wrap frames) demands all four fixes plus careful boundary arithmetic

expected_failure_modes: Agent fixes zigzag and varint bugs by reading decoder.py but misses framer.py ring-buffer wrap because it only manifests at runtime with large captures, not by reading the file

Agent fixes three bugs but misidentifies the Adler-32 scope (reads the spec loosely, assumes 'payload' means the right thing, tests only with short frames where length-prefix is 1 byte so the omitted byte is always 0x01 and Adler-32 happens to match)
Agent generates test vectors with the encoder but uses only small positive values, so zigzag and large-varint bugs do not surface in self-tests, submits with those bugs unfixed

Agent patches decoder.py to handle known captures in /app/captures/ by special-casing observed byte sequences rather than fixing the underlying algorithm, passes captures but fails fresh hidden inputs
Agent fixes varint loop to allow 7 bytes but uses the wrong termination condition (checks bit 7 instead of reading until no continuation bit), producing off-by-one on 7-byte boundary values

speedrun: # In decoder.py: identify zigzag bug — (n >> 1) ^ -(n & 1) on unsigned, fix with masking
# In decoder.py: identify varint loop range(4) → range(7), fix continuation byte limit
# In decoder.py: identify Adler-32 called on payload only, fix to include version+length_prefix_bytes
# In framer.py: read _find_magic, identify off-by-one in wrap boundary index, fix (wrap_pos+1)%size → correct offset
sed/edit decoder.py: fix varint loop to range(7)
sed/edit framer.py: fix ring-buffer wrap index arithmetic
python -I -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'/app/codec'); from encoder import encode; ...round-trip test with negative and large values"
invalid_failure_risks: The 'observe_not_read' difficulty lever is mislabeled — all four bugs are directly visible in the source by reading decoder.py and framer.py; no runtime-only discovery is required, contradicting the stated difficulty mechanism

The Adler-32 scope fix requires the solver to correctly determine which bytes are included per spec; if the spec wording is ambiguous about whether 'version byte' is separate from 'payload', solvers might fix it differently and still pass some but not all corpus cases — potential grading ambiguity

The framer.py wrap bug description says 'off-by-one in index arithmetic' which is directly readable; if a solver fixes it in a slightly different but functionally equivalent way (e.g. rewriting _find_magic cleanly), the verifier must accept any correct implementation, not just the specific patch

The 4096-byte ring-buffer wrap test requires frames positioned at exact byte offsets; if the hidden corpus generator has any off-by-one in how it positions frames relative to the buffer boundary, some ring-buffer tests could be flaky

The internal hint states the zigzag bug 'on an already-int Python value without masking, so for large unsigned n the XOR produces wrong results' — but Python integers are arbitrary precision and `-(n & 1)` for odd n gives -1, so `(n >> 1) ^ -1` in Python produces ~(n>>1) which is correct for two's complement interpretation; the bug description may be inaccurate for Python specifically, potentially making the zigzag code actually correct in Python, undermining that bug
review.reasons: The speedrun reaches a plausible solution in ~19 commands because all four bugs are directly readable in the source files (decoder.py and framer.py), contradicting the 'observe_not_read' tag and pushing genuine_difficulty to 2, which fails the acceptance threshold of 4. Additionally, the zigzag bug description may be technically incorrect for Python's arbitrary-precision integers — `(n >> 1) ^ -(n & 1)` in Python is actually the correct zigzag formula since `-1` in Python XOR works as expected for any bit width — meaning one of the four planted bugs may not exist as described, which would undermine test reliability.
fixes: To increase genuine_difficulty to 4+: make at least two bugs only manifest at runtime and not be visible by reading the source — for example, the framer wrap bug could be hidden in a C extension or in logic that looks correct statically but fails due to mutable state across calls; or require the solver to discover bugs by instrumenting a running daemon, not by static reading

Verify and correct the zigzag bug description for Python: in Python, `(n >> 1) ^ -(n & 1)` IS the correct zigzag decode formula because Python integers have no fixed width; to plant a real bug, use something like `(n >> 1) ^ (-(n & 1) & 0xFFFFFFFF)` which truncates the mask and fails for large values, or use `(n >> 1) - (n & 1)` which is wrong

Replace the 'observe_not_read' lever with a genuinely runtime-only failure: e.g., the ring-buffer bug only surfaces when the framer is called with actual streaming chunks (not a full buffer at once), requiring the solver to run the CLI on large captures or write a streaming test harness rather than reading the code

Add a requirement that the solver must not modify the reference encoder, and make the verifier test that encoder.py is unchanged — this prevents solvers from 'fixing' the round-trip by changing both sides
Clarify the Adler-32 spec wording unambiguously: spell out exactly which bytes (with byte offsets from frame start) are included in the checksum computation, to eliminate grading disputes

verdicts.reason: DNA storage codec involves erasure coding and sequence reconstruction over a deletion channel, not binary frame parsing with varints and checksums.

Both tasks involve fixing a binary frame decoder that silently corrupts or drops frames, with the core challenge being correct field parsing and edge-case handling, though the candidate adds varint encoding, zigzag signing, Adler-32 checksum, and ring-buffer wrap complexity.
Cell lineage reconstruction is a computer vision and biology problem entirely unrelated to binary protocol decoding.
AES-CTR SQLite cipher repair involves cryptographic nonce derivation bugs in a C library, not varint/length-prefix binary frame parsing.
The WAL audit service involves HMAC computation over canonical binary records and refund resolution, not variable-length integer decoding or frame checksum verification.
